title: CFD-DEM Investigation on Heat and Mass Transfer of Ellipsoidal Particles Drying in a Bladed Mixer with Toroidal Blades

authors.affiliation: Department of Mechanical Engineering, Brawijaya University
authors.name: Sri Utami Handayani

authors.affiliation: Department of Mechanical Engineering, Brawijaya University
authors.name: Hadi Wahyudi

abstract: Conventional blade geometries in bladed mixers create non-uniform temperature and moisture distributions during particle drying, leading to inconsistent product quality and extended processing times. This study investigates a novel toroidal blade geometry for enhancing heat and mass transfer during drying of ellipsoidal food and pharmaceutical particles. We combined experimental measurements with coupled CFD-DEM simulations to analyze flow patterns, temperature evolution, and moisture removal rates. The toroidal blade assembly (major diameter 120 mm, tube diameter 20 mm) was tested at rotational speeds of 30, 60, and 90 RPM with inlet air temperatures of 60, 80, and 100Â°C. Approximately 50,000 ellipsoidal particles (aspect ratio 2.0, equivalent diameter 4 mm) representing wheat grains were dried from initial moisture content of 0.25 dry basis. Results show the toroidal design achieved 23.7% faster drying compared to flat blades and 14.2% faster than pitched blades at 90 RPM and 100Â°C. The mixing index improved by 31% over flat blades, reducing moisture content standard deviation from 0.047 to 0.032 at 180 seconds. Specific energy consumption decreased by 18.4% compared to conventional designs. Model validation against experimental data yielded RMSE values below 0.015 for moisture content predictions. This work provides the first comprehensive CFD-DEM analysis of non-spherical particle drying with toroidal blades, demonstrating practical advantages for food processing and pharmaceutical manufacturing applications.

content.text: In 2023, the global food processing industry lost an estimated $4.2 billion to product quality inconsistencies traced directly to non-uniform drying in batch mixers (Handayani et al., 2023). Pharmaceutical manufacturers face similar challenges -- moisture content variations of just 2% can trigger batch rejection under FDA guidelines, costing upwards of $150,000 per failed production run. The root cause? Conventional blade geometries create dead zones and preferential flow paths that leave some particles over-dried while others remain too wet.

Existing approaches to particle drying in bladed mixers rely primarily on flat or pitched blade configurations. Pratama Herman et al. (2022) demonstrated that ellipsoidal particles in flat-blade mixers exhibit segregation patterns with mixing indices below 0.65 after 300 seconds of operation. Their DEM simulations revealed that particle aspect ratio significantly affects circulation patterns, though they didn't examine heat transfer or drying performance. Rafiq et al. (2025) investigated polydispersity effects on heat transfer in bladed mixers using spherical particles, achieving Nusselt numbers ranging from 12.3 to 18.7 depending on size distribution. The limitation here is clear: their soft-sphere DEM model assumed perfect spheres, which doesn't capture the rotational dynamics and contact mechanics of real agricultural or pharmaceutical particles. BruchmuÂ¨ller et al. (2010) modeled coffee bean drying in fluidized beds with resolved 1D temperature profiles within each particle, reporting local temperature gradients up to 15Â°C across a single bean. But fluidized beds operate under fundamentally different flow regimes than mechanically agitated mixers -- the convective heat transfer coefficients they measured (45-67 W/mÂ²K) don't translate to blade-driven systems where particle-particle contact dominates.

The gap becomes obvious when you look at what's missing: nobody's systematically studied how blade geometry affects drying uniformity for non-spherical particles. We know ellipsoidal particles behave differently than spheres (He & Tafti, 2017), and we know blade shape matters for mixing (Pratama Herman et al., 2022), but the intersection -- blade design optimized specifically for drying ellipsoidal particles -- remains unexplored. Toroidal blade geometry offers a promising alternative because the closed-loop structure generates continuous circulation without the sharp edges that cause particle attrition in pitched blade designs.

This paper presents the first comprehensive CFD-DEM investigation of ellipsoidal particle drying in a bladed mixer equipped with toroidal blades. Our contributions are:
\u2022 Development and validation of a coupled CFD-DEM framework for non-spherical particle drying with multi-sphere approximation (5 spheres per ellipsoid) and shrinking core moisture model
\u2022 Experimental characterization of toroidal blade performance across rotational speeds (30-90 RPM) and air temperatures (60-100Â°C) with 50,000 wheat-grain-equivalent particles
\u2022 Quantitative comparison against flat and pitched blade configurations showing 23.7% faster drying and 31% improved mixing homogeneity
\u2022 Energy efficiency analysis demonstrating 18.4% reduction in specific energy consumption compared to conventional designs

Section II reviews related work on CFD-DEM coupling methods, particle drying fundamentals, and blade geometry effects. Section III describes the experimental apparatus, particle characterization, and measurement protocols. Section IV presents the mathematical models including CFD governing equations, DEM particle dynamics, and coupled heat-mass transfer formulations. Section V analyzes flow patterns, temperature evolution, drying performance, and model validation. Section VI concludes with practical implications and future research directions.

Three distinct research threads converge in this work: CFD-DEM coupling methodologies for multiphase systems, heat and mass transfer mechanisms in particle drying, and the influence of blade geometry on mixing and thermal performance. Understanding how these threads connect -- and where they leave gaps -- is essential for positioning the toroidal blade investigation.

section2a.title: CFD-DEM Coupling Methods for Particle Systems

content.text: The CFD-DEM approach treats the continuous gas phase with Eulerian conservation equations while tracking individual particles through Lagrangian dynamics. Wang & Shen (2022) developed a coarse-grained CFD-DEM model for dense gas-solid reacting flows, achieving computational speedups of 15-20x by grouping particles into parcels while maintaining accuracy within 8% of fully resolved simulations. Their method handled particle volume fractions up to 0.55, but the coarse-graining introduced errors in contact force calculations that became significant when particle shapes deviated from spheres. Adhav et al. (2023) validated a partitioned coupling interface for heat and mass transfer using OpenFOAM and LIGGGHTS, demonstrating that explicit coupling with time step ratios of 1:10 (CFD:DEM) maintained stability for Stokes numbers below 5. The limitation: their validation cases used only spherical glass beads in simple geometries, leaving open questions about coupling stability for ellipsoidal particles in complex blade-driven flows. Wang et al. (2020) proposed a semi-resolved CFD-DEM method where particles larger than 3 grid cells are resolved individually while smaller particles use drag correlations. This hybrid approach captured thermal boundary layers around particles with 12% higher accuracy than fully unresolved methods, though at 3.2x higher computational cost. What's interesting here is that the accuracy gain came primarily from resolving the wake structure behind particles -- which suggests that ellipsoidal particles, with their orientation-dependent drag, might benefit even more from semi-resolved treatment.

content.Title: CFD-DEM Coupling Framework for Ellipsoidal Particle Drying
content.caption: Fig. 1.

content.text: Fig. 1 illustrates the coupling framework used in this study. The CFD solver operates on a fixed Eulerian grid with time step $\Delta t_{\mathrm{CFD}} = 1 \times 10^{-4}$ s, while the DEM solver tracks individual particles with $\Delta t_{\mathrm{DEM}} = 1 \times 10^{-5}$ s. This 1:10 ratio ensures that particle collisions are resolved accurately even at high rotational speeds. The coupling interface exchanges void fraction and velocity fields downward to DEM, and drag forces plus heat transfer rates upward to CFD. Iteration continues until both solvers converge within specified tolerances (residuals below $1 \times 10^{-5}$ for CFD, force imbalance below $1 \times 10^{-6}$ N for DEM).

Li et al. (2026) applied multiscale CFD-DEM to metal particle deposition in molten salt, using a three-level grid refinement strategy that resolved near-wall regions at 0.1 mm while maintaining 2 mm cells in the bulk flow. Their simulations captured deposition rates within 15% of experimental measurements, though the molten salt's high viscosity (0.03 PaÂ·s) simplified the turbulence modeling compared to gas-phase drying. Gou & Shen (2026) leveraged GPU acceleration to simulate 2 million particles in a fluidized bed reactor, achieving real-time factors of 0.8 (simulation runs 20% slower than real time) on an NVIDIA A100. The GPU implementation reduced memory bandwidth bottlenecks by storing particle data in shared memory, but the method required particles to remain within local GPU memory blocks, which limits applicability to systems with long-range particle transport like bladed mixers. Jia et al. (2026) investigated pressurized fluidization at 0.5-2.0 MPa using CFD-DEM, finding that increased pressure enhanced heat transfer coefficients by 40-65% due to higher gas density and thermal conductivity. Their work revealed that the Nusselt number correlation $\mathrm{Nu} = 2 + 0.6 \mathrm{Re}^{0.5} \mathrm{Pr}^{0.33}$ underpredicted heat transfer at elevated pressures, requiring a pressure correction factor $(P/P_0)^{0.25}$ to match experimental data. This pressure dependence isn't directly relevant to atmospheric drying, but it highlights how standard correlations can fail outside their calibration range -- a caution that applies equally to ellipsoidal particles where most correlations assume spheres.

VÃ¤likangas et al. (2020) coupled soft-sphere DEM with CFD to model dry particle deposition on fin-and-tube heat exchangers, tracking 150,000 particles over 60 seconds of simulation time. Their results showed that particle rebound coefficients below 0.3 led to rapid fouling, while coefficients above 0.6 maintained clean surfaces through self-cleaning collisions. The soft-sphere model used here -- with normal stiffness $k_n = 800$ N/m and damping coefficient $\gamma_n = 0.3$ -- is similar to what we adopt for wheat grain particles, though our ellipsoidal geometry requires additional rotational damping to prevent unrealistic spinning. Zhang & Liu (2025) simulated atomic layer deposition on cohesive porous particles during fluidization, incorporating van der Waals forces and surface reaction kinetics into the CFD-DEM framework. The cohesive forces (adhesion energy 0.05 mJ/mÂ²) dominated particle dynamics at sizes below 50 Î¼m, but for the 4 mm particles in our study, cohesion is negligible compared to gravitational and contact forces.

section2b.title: Heat and Mass Transfer in Particle Drying

content.text: Drying of particulate materials involves simultaneous heat and mass transfer with phase change, complicated by particle shrinkage, internal moisture gradients, and temperature-dependent transport properties. Mezhericher et al. (2009) developed a comprehensive model for heat and mass transfer with particle breakage during spray drying, showing that thermal stress-induced cracking occurred when internal moisture gradients exceeded 0.15 kg/kg across a particle diameter. Their model predicted breakage rates within 20% of experimental observations for ceramic particles, though the brittle fracture mechanics they used don't apply to the elastic-plastic behavior of food particles. Handayani et al. (2023) investigated ellipsoidal particle drying in fluidized beds using CFD-DEM with resolved internal temperature profiles, reporting that aspect ratio 2.0 particles dried 12% faster than equivalent-volume spheres due to increased surface area. The effective diffusivity they measured -- $D_{\mathrm{eff}} = 2.3 \times 10^{-9}$ mÂ²/s at 80Â°C for wheat grains -- serves as a baseline for our model calibration. What's notable is that their fluidized bed operated at superficial velocities of 1.2-1.8 m/s, creating convective heat transfer coefficients of 85-120 W/mÂ²K, significantly higher than the 35-55 W/mÂ²K we expect in the bladed mixer where particle-gas relative velocities are lower.

Dorri et al. (1985) examined drying of wood particles with longitudinal mass transfer using three numerical approaches: a frontal model tracking the drying front position, a volume-averaged smeared model, and an equivalent spherical particle model. The frontal model matched experimental data best (RMSE 0.008 kg/kg) but required tracking the moving boundary, while the smeared model was computationally cheaper but overpredicted drying rates by 15-25% in the falling rate period. For our ellipsoidal particles, the smeared approach is more practical given the need to simulate 50,000 particles simultaneously. BiaÅobrzewski et al. (2008) simulated carrot cube drying in a spout-fluidized bed, accounting for particle shrinkage that reduced dimensions by up to 35% during drying from 4.5 to 0.1 kg/kg dry basis. Their shrinkage model -- volume proportional to moisture content raised to power 0.85 -- introduced numerical challenges when particles became too small relative to the CFD grid, requiring dynamic grid refinement. We avoid this complexity by limiting our study to partial drying (0.25 to 0.05 kg/kg) where shrinkage remains below 10%.

Nganhou (2003) studied heat and mass transfer through thick beds of cocoa beans, measuring effective thermal conductivity of 0.18-0.24 W/mK depending on moisture content and bed porosity. The bed-scale effective diffusivity was 2-3 orders of magnitude higher than single-particle diffusivity due to convective transport between particles, highlighting the importance of resolving particle-scale flow in our CFD-DEM model. Beigi (2016) investigated vacuum drying of celeriac, finding that reduced pressure (10-30 kPa) increased effective diffusivity by 40-60% compared to atmospheric drying, though the energy cost of maintaining vacuum offset the time savings for most applications. Nadi & Tzempelikos (2018) characterized vacuum drying of apple slices, reporting activation energies of 28.3 kJ/mol for moisture diffusion and 42.7 kJ/mol for shrinkage, with the higher shrinkage activation energy indicating that structural changes lag behind moisture removal. These activation energies inform our temperature-dependent property correlations.

Dobre et al. (2016) analyzed fixed bed drying of non-deformable porous particles, deriving analytical solutions for the coupled heat and mass transfer equations under constant drying rate conditions. Their solutions showed that the Biot number for mass transfer ($\mathrm{Bi}_m = h_m R / D_{\mathrm{eff}}$, where $h_m$ is the mass transfer coefficient, $R$ is particle radius, and $D_{\mathrm{eff}}$ is effective diffusivity) must exceed 10 for internal diffusion to limit drying rates. For our 4 mm particles with $D_{\mathrm{eff}} \approx 2 \times 10^{-9}$ mÂ²/s and $h_m \approx 0.02$ m/s, $\mathrm{Bi}_m \approx 20$, confirming that internal diffusion controls the falling rate period. Liapis & Bruttini (2009) developed a mathematical model for spray freeze drying of frozen particles in trays, incorporating sublimation kinetics and heat transfer through the porous dried layer. Their model predicted drying times within 15% of experimental values for pharmaceutical particles, though the freeze-drying mechanism (sublimation) differs fundamentally from the evaporation we're studying.

section2c.title: Blade Geometry Effects on Mixing and Heat Transfer

content.text: Blade geometry profoundly influences flow patterns, mixing efficiency, and heat transfer in mechanically agitated systems, yet most studies focus on liquid mixing or spherical particles. Shahbazi et al. (2021) optimized SMX static mixer thermal and hydraulic performance using CFD coupled with genetic algorithms, achieving 18% improvement in heat transfer coefficient while reducing pressure drop by 12% through blade angle optimization (optimal angle 45Â° vs. standard 60Â°). The limitation: static mixers operate under continuous flow with no moving parts, so their optimization criteria (pressure drop minimization) don't translate to batch bladed mixers where power consumption depends on blade-particle collisions. Shahsavandi et al. (2026) analyzed flexible-baffles millimeter-scale mixers with C-shaped obstacles using coupled CFD-FSI, showing that baffle flexibility improved mixing by 25% through chaotic advection induced by baffle oscillations. But the Reynolds numbers in their microfluidic system (Re = 10-100) place it firmly in the laminar regime, whereas our bladed mixer operates at Re = 5000-15000 where turbulence dominates.

Meng et al. (2026) investigated a fish-tail bionic static mixer experimentally and numerically, finding that the biomimetic geometry reduced mixing length by 30% compared to helical mixers while maintaining pressure drop within 5% of the baseline. The fish-tail design created counter-rotating vortex pairs that enhanced radial mixing, a mechanism potentially relevant to toroidal blades which also generate toroidal vortices. Ein-Mozaffari & Hashemi (2019) studied gas dispersion in highly viscous fluids using a coaxial mixer, employing electrical resistance tomography to visualize gas holdup distributions. Their results showed that the coaxial configuration (central impeller + anchor) achieved 40% higher gas holdup than single impeller systems, though the high viscosity (10-50 PaÂ·s) makes direct comparison to gas-particle systems difficult.

Hoffmann et al. (2022) used CFD to analyze flow resistance in randomly packed beds of crushed rock and ellipsoidal particles, deriving a modified Ergun equation with shape factor correction: $\Delta P / L = 150 \mu U (1-\epsilon)^2 / (\phi^2 d_p^2 \epsilon^3) + 1.75 \rho U^2 (1-\epsilon) / (\phi d_p \epsilon^3)$, where $\phi$ is the sphericity (0.65 for crushed rock, 0.85 for ellipsoids with aspect ratio 2.0). This shape correction is crucial for accurate drag force calculations in our DEM model. Hoffmann (2021) extended this work to determine flow resistance in crushed rock beds using a CFD/DEM approach, finding that particle angularity increased pressure drop by 35-50% compared to smooth ellipsoids at the same porosity. The implication: our smooth ellipsoidal approximation likely underpredicts drag forces for real wheat grains with surface roughness.

Ahmadi Motlagh & Hashemabadi (2008a) performed 3D CFD simulations of particle-to-fluid heat transfer in randomly packed beds of cylindrical particles, validating against experimental data with RMSE below 8% for Nusselt numbers ranging from 15 to 45. Their correlation $\mathrm{Nu} = 2.1 + 0.52 \mathrm{Re}^{0.55} \mathrm{Pr}^{0.33}$ for cylindrical particles shows 15-20% higher heat transfer than the standard Ranz-Marshall correlation for spheres at the same Reynolds number, suggesting that non-spherical geometry enhances heat transfer through increased surface area and flow disturbance. Ahmadi Motlagh & Hashemabadi (2008b) evaluated heat transfer coefficients from cylindrical particles using CFD, reporting that particle orientation relative to flow direction changed Nusselt numbers by up to 40% (Nu = 18.3 for flow parallel to cylinder axis vs. Nu = 25.7 for perpendicular flow at Re = 100). This orientation dependence is exactly what we need to capture with our multi-sphere ellipsoidal model. Mirhashemi & Hashemabadi (2012) studied wall effects on heat transfer for orderly stacked cylindrical particles in tube channels, finding that wall proximity increased local Nusselt numbers by 25-35% within one particle diameter of the wall due to flow acceleration in the gap. Our toroidal blade geometry creates similar near-wall regions where enhanced heat transfer is expected.

The experimental investigation combined a custom-built bladed mixer with instrumentation for temperature, moisture content, and power consumption measurements. Parallel CFD-DEM simulations used the validated framework to extend the parameter space beyond experimental constraints. This section describes the apparatus, particle characterization, measurement protocols, and operating conditions.

section3a.title: Experimental Apparatus and Toroidal Blade Design

content.text: The bladed mixer consists of a cylindrical stainless steel vessel (300 mm inner diameter, 250 mm height, wall thickness 3 mm) with a transparent polycarbonate lid for visual observation. The toroidal blade assembly mounts on a central vertical shaft (20 mm diameter) driven by a variable-speed motor (0.75 kW, 0-200 RPM). Each toroidal blade forms a closed loop with major diameter $D_{\mathrm{major}} = 120$ mm and tube diameter $d_{\mathrm{tube}} = 20$ mm, fabricated from stainless steel tubing (AISI 304, thermal conductivity 16.2 W/mK). Four blades are positioned at 90Â° intervals around the shaft, with vertical spacing of 50 mm between blade centers. The toroidal geometry was chosen because preliminary flow visualization showed it generates continuous circulation without the dead zones observed in flat blade configurations. Heated air enters through a perforated distributor plate at the vessel bottom (hole diameter 3 mm, 25% open area) and exits through a filter at the top.

content.Title: Toroidal Blade Mixer Experimental Setup
content.caption: Fig. 2.

content.text: Fig. 2 shows the experimental setup. Temperature sensors (K-type thermocouples, Â±0.5Â°C accuracy) are positioned at three heights (50, 125, and 200 mm from the distributor plate) to monitor vertical temperature profiles. A torque sensor (HBM T20WN, 0-20 Nm range, 0.05% accuracy) measures shaft torque for power consumption calculations. The motor speed is controlled via a variable frequency drive with feedback from an optical encoder (1000 pulses per revolution). Heated air is supplied by a 3 kW electric heater with PID temperature control (Â±1Â°C setpoint accuracy). Air flow rate is measured by a thermal mass flow meter (Bronkhorst F-201CV, 0-100 L/min range, Â±1% reading accuracy). Moisture content is determined by extracting particle samples through a sampling port at 30-second intervals and analyzing them with a halogen moisture analyzer (Mettler Toledo HB43-S, 0.001 g resolution, 0.05% moisture accuracy).

The toroidal blade geometry creates a fundamentally different flow pattern compared to flat or pitched blades. As the blade rotates, particles are lifted along the outer surface of the torus, then released at the top where they fall back into the bed. This continuous circulation minimizes stagnant regions. The closed-loop structure also eliminates the sharp trailing edges found in flat blades, reducing particle attrition -- a critical consideration for fragile pharmaceutical pellets or food products where breakage affects quality.

Wheat grains (Triticum aestivum, variety Giza 168) were selected as model particles due to their ellipsoidal geometry, well-documented drying behavior, and relevance to food processing applications. Particle dimensions were measured using digital calipers (Mitutoyo CD-6" CS, 0.01 mm resolution) on a sample of 200 grains. The average major axis length is $a = 6.8 \pm 0.4$ mm, minor axis $b = 3.4 \pm 0.3$ mm, giving an aspect ratio of 2.0. The equivalent spherical diameter is $d_{\mathrm{eq}} = (ab^2)^{1/3} = 4.3$ mm. Particle density was measured by water displacement (Archimedes method) at three moisture contents: $\rho_p = 1320$ kg/mÂ³ at 0.25 kg/kg dry basis (initial), $\rho_p = 1280$ kg/mÂ³ at 0.15 kg/kg, and $\rho_p = 1240$ kg/mÂ³ at 0.05 kg/kg (final). The density decrease reflects moisture loss
